newsitem.title: FRANCE: What to expect from French public finances audit.
newsitem.headline: What to expect from French public finances audit.

text.p: An audit of public finances ordered by France's new Socialist-led government is due to be completed on July 21. The government has said the results will be published immediately.
Following are details of the motives for holding the audit, who is conducting it, and what to expect.
The government says it wants full details of the state of public finances before deciding on any measures it needs to take to curb the public deficit in preparation for monetary union.

It is following an example set by former prime minister Edouard Balladur in 1993, who had an audit carried out after the centre-right regained power to establish the state of public finances left behind by five years of Socialist government.

The conservative opposition has accused the government of hiding behind the audit for political reasons, either to show French people why it is forced to break election promises to end austerity because of a higher-than-expected deficit, or to show France's European partners how hard it will be to cut the deficit in preparation for monetary union.

Conservative parliamentarian and budget expert Philippe Auberger said on July 2 there was no need for the audit. "This is a political audit, it has nothing to do with the situation of public finances," he told reporters.

The audit is being carried out by two members of the independent Court of Auditors, Philippe Nasse and Jacques Bonnet, who will work with finance ministry civil servants to forecast the total public deficit -- which covers central and local authority spending and welfare spending.
Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has said first indications have suggested French public finances are in a "serious" condition.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said the audit was likely to show the total public deficit was significantly higher than the 3.0 percent of gross domestic product forecast in the 1997 Finance Act.

The audit will say where the deficit would be at the end of the year without corrective action. Strauss-Kahn has said measures to curb the deficit by a few decimal points will be taken if there is a significant overshoot.
It is unclear whether the auditors will provide a range of deficit/GDP ratio forecasts, dependent on economic growth and other factors, or simply give one single figure.

The government has declined to give a precise figure for the deficit/GDP ratio it expects from the audit. But Strauss-Kahn said newspaper and other reports were forecasting the deficit at between 3.4 and 3.8 percent of GDP.
The auditors are expected to give a revised figure for the central government budget deficit, forecast in the 1997 Finance Act at 284 billion francs.

It will also give a new figure for the welfare deficit, which the previous government had aimed to limit to 30 billion francs, though it acknowledged earlier this year it would be 35 billion due to a slower-than-expected rise in total wages. The welfare system uses payroll taxes to fund healthcare, pensions and family benefits.
To provide a complete picture of public finances, the auditors would also need to calculate the potential surplus or shortfall in national unemployment fund UNEDIC and in local authority budgets.
